title: Formal occasions
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: valē HAS BEEN IN YOUR MOUTH SINCE THE SECOND MODULE OF THIS COURSE, AND THIS IS THE SAME WORD AT THE OTHER END OF A LIFE. L1-M2 taught it as an everyday goodbye; avē atque valē is Catullus over his brother's ashes, and nothing about the word has changed except the occasion. atque rather than et, because L1-M10's heavier conjunction is what a funeral formula takes — which is a REGISTER error to get wrong and not a grammatical one, and that distinction is what this module is about.

THE ECCLESIASTICAL REGISTER IS AT HOME HERE AND NOWHERE ELSE IN THIS COURSE. requiēscat in pāce is not classical Latin: it is liturgical, it is the Latin most English speakers have actually seen, and a condolence is the one occasion where it is the right thing to say. M1 of this level refused it for exactly that reason — a saying and a liturgical formula are different things. Its sound line is also the one place in the course where the ECCLESIASTICAL pronunciation is the correct reading rather than one option of three.

A BARE SUBJUNCTIVE IS A WISH, AND THAT IS THE FOURTH JOB THESE ENDINGS DO. L3-M4 opened the present subjunctive for conditions, purpose and advice; L4-M5 added the potential 'might'; requiēscat and sit here have nothing in front of them at all and mean 'may he rest' and 'may it be'. L4-M3's utinam was the same wish WITH a particle, so this module simply removes it.

A FORMAL OCCASION IN LATIN RUNS ALMOST ENTIRELY ON THE DATIVE. Thanks are given TO somebody (grātiās tibi agō), health is wished TO somebody (bene tibi), peace is TO somebody (pāx tibi sit) — and S10 has tibi three times doing the same job. L1-M1 opened the case with mihi nōmen est and nothing since has leaned on it this hard. bene tibi is also a whole toast with no verb in it, which is L4-M7's sign discipline at a happier moment: leave out what the occasion supplies.

grātiās agō COSTS NOTHING NEW AND L1-M2 COULD NOT WRITE IT. That module taught grātiās as a bare thanks and agō as 'I do', and the full construction is both of them plus a dative — so a formal thanks is three words this course has had since its second module, in an arrangement it was too early to build. The plate is the accusative where the dative belongs, because after forty-nine modules a person after a verb is an object by reflex.

THE VOCATIVE'S SECOND USE IS FORMAL ADDRESS, TWO RUNGS AFTER ITS FIRST. M2 opened it as mock address — ō stulte — and a speech addresses its audience with the identical shape. A case whose whole job is tone is honestly taught by showing both ends of it, and ō is optional in both: in M2 it carried a joke and here it heightens.

YOU ADDRESS THE LIVING, AND THAT IS WHY S08 WRITES Mārcus AND NOT Mārce. The module has just taught the vocative's formal use and this sentence declines it, because the man is dead. mortuus est is L2-M8's participle-as-adjective arrangement — 'he is dead', hence 'he has died' — and the choice of case is the kind of thing a register module can show and a grammar cannot.

words.note: 'Hail' — a greeting for an arrival, and the formal counterpart of L1-M2's salvē. With valē it is Catullus's farewell to his brother.
'And' — L1-M10's word, and the lexicalised one-word form, not a seam. It is heavier than et, which is why a farewell takes it.
'Be well' — L1-M2's word, taught in the second module of this course as an everyday goodbye. Here it is half of a farewell to the dead.

sentences.trap: valē has been in your mouth since the second module of this course, and this is the same word at the other end of a life. L1-M2 taught it as 'bye'; Catullus wrote it over his brother's ashes — and nothing about the word changed, only the occasion.
sentences.sound: A-vē AT-que VA-lē. Six syllables and two long ē sounds, one closing each greeting.

variations.changed: M2's vocative between them, which is formal address rather than a joke

mistake.why: et where atque belongs. Both mean 'and' and atque is the heavier — L1-M10 taught it as the lexicalised form — and a funeral formula takes the weight. This is not a grammatical error but a register one, which is what this module is about.

sentences.usage: Catullus 101, over his brother's ashes. Classical verse, and the most quoted farewell in Latin.
sentences.mnemonic: The same valē as L1-M2, forty-eight rungs on.

words.note: 'May he rest' — a present subjunctive, L3-M4's mood, used as a wish. This is LITURGICAL Latin and not classical: it is the Latin most English speakers have actually seen.
'In' plus the ablative. L1-M7's preposition, and here it is a state rather than a place.
'Peace' — pāx as the subject, pāce after in. English 'pacify' and 'Pacific' come from it.

sentences.trap: THIS IS LITURGICAL LATIN AND NOT CLASSICAL, and the module says so because it is the Latin most English speakers have actually seen. requiēscat is a present subjunctive — L3-M4's mood — used as a WISH, which is the same job utinam did at L4-M3 with no particle in front of it.
sentences.sound: Restored classical: re-kwi-ES-kat in PAH-ke. Ecclesiastical: re-kwi-ES-kat in PAH-che — and the ecclesiastical is the tradition this phrase actually belongs to, which makes it the one sentence in the course where that reading is the right one.

variations.changed: more than one, so the verb goes plural

variations.cue: May he rest in peace, Marcus.
variations.changed: M2's vocative, addressing the dead
a plain statement instead of a wish

sentences.usage: Liturgical, and on more headstones than any other Latin. Ecclesiastical register.
sentences.mnemonic: A subjunctive with no particle is a wish.

words.note: 'Well'. L1-M2's adverb, and it takes no ending. Here it is a whole toast with no verb at all.
'To you' — the dative. L2-M1's row, and the case a toast needs: the good health goes TO somebody.

sentences.trap: Two words, no verb, and a whole toast. Latin will raise a glass with an adverb and a dative and leave everything else to the occasion — which is L4-M7's sign-Latin discipline applied to a happier moment: leave out whatever the situation supplies.
sentences.sound: BE-ne TI-bi. Four short syllables and not one long vowel — the lightest formal sentence in the course.

variations.changed: the dative of the speaker, which is a joke and not a toast
M2's vocative, in formal address

variations.cue: The best of health to you.
variations.changed: L1-M2's superlative adverb, which is warmer

sentences.usage: Said raising a glass. Classical and still used.
sentences.mnemonic: An adverb and a dative make a toast.

words.note: 'Thanks' — plural always, and there is no singular of it in this use. L1-M2's word, and there it was a bare grātiās.
'To you' — the dative, which is who the thanks are given to.
'I do, I drive' — and with grātiās it is 'I give thanks'. L1-M2's verb, in a fixed phrase that module could not yet build.

sentences.trap: L1-M2 taught grātiās as a bare thanks and agō as 'I do'. The full construction is both of them plus a dative, and this course has had all three words since its second module — so the formal thanks costs nothing new and is simply the arrangement that module was too early to write.
sentences.sound: GRĀ-ti-ās TI-bi A-gō. Seven syllables and three long vowels.

variations.changed: no dative, which is less formal and commoner
L2-M6's plural, which is what an institution says
L1-M2's bare form, which is everyday

mistake.why: the object shape where the dative belongs. The thanks are given TO you, so tibi — and after forty-nine modules the accusative is the reflex for a person after a verb, which is what makes the dative construction worth a plate.

sentences.usage: Said formally, in a speech or a letter.
sentences.mnemonic: Thanks go TO somebody: tibi, not tē.

words.note: 'O' — the particle of address, M2's word. In formal Latin it is optional and slightly heightening; in M2 it carried a joke.
'Marcus' as ADDRESS — M2's vocative, and this is its SECOND use. There it was mock address; here it is a speech addressing its audience, and the shape is identical.
'Hail' — a greeting for an arrival, and the formal counterpart of L1-M2's salvē. With valē it is Catullus's farewell to his brother.

sentences.trap: THE VOCATIVE'S SECOND USE, two rungs after its first. M2 opened it as a joke — ō stulte — and a speech addresses its audience with the same shape. A case whose whole job is tone is honestly taught by showing both ends of it, and this module is the other end.
sentences.sound: Ō MĀR-ce, A-vē. Six syllables and three long vowels: a formal address is slow.

variations.changed: the farewell instead of the greeting
ō dropped, which is plainer and still formal
M2's insult in M4's frame, which is a joke about registers

sentences.mnemonic: The same shape as M2's joke, at the other register.

sentences.display: Grātiās tibi agō, ō Mārce; bene tibi.
sentences.cue: I give you my thanks, Marcus; good health to you.
sentences.literal: thanks to-you I-give O Marcus! well to-you

words.note: 'Thanks' — plural always. L1-M2's word.
'To you' — the dative.
'I do' — and with grātiās, 'I give thanks'. L1-M2's verb.
'O' — the particle of address.
'Marcus' as address — M2's vocative in its formal use.
'Well'. L1-M2's adverb, and here a toast.
'To you' — the dative, twice in one sentence and doing the same job both times.

sentences.trap: tibi twice, and it is the same case doing the same job. Thanks are given to somebody and health is wished to somebody — so a formal occasion in Latin runs almost entirely on the dative, which L1-M1 opened with mihi nōmen est and which nothing since has used this heavily.
sentences.sound: GRĀ-ti-ās TI-bi A-gō, Ō MĀR-ce; BE-ne TI-bi. Thirteen syllables and five long vowels.

variations.cue: I give you my thanks; good health to you.
variations.changed: the address dropped

variations.display: Grātiās tibi agimus, ō Mārce; bene tibi.
variations.cue: We give you our thanks, Marcus; good health to you.
variations.changed: L2-M6's plural, which is what a group says

variations.cue: Good health to you, Marcus; thanks.

words.note: 'Peace' as the subject — pāce after in. English 'pacify' comes from it.
'To you' — the dative, and the peace goes to you as the health did.
'May it be' — sum's present subjunctive, L3-M4's mood, used as a WISH. The same job requiēscat does, with no particle in front of either.

sentences.trap: A subjunctive as a wish, for the second time in this module. L3-M4 opened the mood for conditions, purpose and advice; L4-M5 added the potential 'might'; and a bare subjunctive with nothing in front of it is a wish — which is the fourth job the same endings do and the one a formal occasion needs.
sentences.sound: Restored classical: PAHKS TI-bi SIT. Ecclesiastical: the same, because pāx has no c before e or i. The long ā is where the weight is.

variations.changed: sit dropped, which is what a liturgical formula does
the other wish, and the other use of pāx
a statement instead of a wish

sentences.usage: Liturgical and classical both. Formal in either register.
sentences.mnemonic: A bare subjunctive is a wish.

sentences.display: Mārcus mortuus est; requiēscat in pāce.
sentences.cue: Marcus has died; may he rest in peace.
sentences.literal: Marcus dead he-is may-he-rest in peace

words.note: A Roman name in the SUBJECT shape — because the sentence talks about him rather than to him. M2's Mārce would be address, and he cannot be addressed now.
'Dead' — a participle used as an ADJECTIVE, agreeing with Mārcus. L2-M8's frāctus est arrangement, and mortuus est is how Latin says 'has died'.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum, es, est, sunt.
'May he rest' — a present subjunctive, L3-M4's mood, used as a wish. This is LITURGICAL Latin and not classical: it is the Latin most English speakers have actually seen.
'In' plus the ablative. L1-M7's preposition.
'Peace' — pāx as the subject, pāce after in. English 'pacify' and 'Pacific' come from it.

sentences.trap: Mārcus and not Mārce, and the reason is the saddest in the course: you address the living. The module has just taught the vocative's formal use and this sentence declines it — which is the kind of thing a register module can show and a grammar cannot.
sentences.sound: MĀR-cus MOR-tu-us EST; re-kwi-ES-kat in PAH-ke. Fourteen syllables, and the ecclesiastical reading of the second half is the right one.

variations.display: Iūlia mortua est; requiēscat in pāce.
variations.cue: Julia has died; may she rest in peace.
variations.changed: a woman, so the participle moves and the verb does not
the wish dropped, which is a report
the negative

sentences.usage: Said announcing a death. Formal, and the second half ecclesiastical.

sentences.display: Avē atque valē, ō Mārce; grātiās tibi agō.
sentences.cue: Hail and farewell, Marcus; I give you my thanks.
sentences.literal: hail and farewell O Marcus! thanks to-you I-give

words.note: 'Hail' — a greeting for an arrival, and the formal counterpart of L1-M2's salvē. With valē it is Catullus's farewell to his brother.
'And' — L1-M10's heavier conjunction, lexicalised as one word.
'Be well' — L1-M2's word, at the other end of a life.
'O' — the particle of address.
'Marcus' as address — M2's vocative in its formal use. Here he can still be addressed.
'Thanks' — plural always. L1-M2's word.
'To you' — the dative.
'I do' — and with grātiās, 'I give thanks'.

sentences.trap: Catullus's formula with a vocative inside it and a thanks after it, and every word is L1's or L2's except avē. That is what a fourth module of a fifth level should look like: the occasion is new and the language is not.
sentences.sound: A-vē AT-que VA-lē, Ō MĀR-ce; GRĀ-ti-ās TI-bi A-gō. Sixteen syllables and seven long vowels — the slowest line in the module.

variations.changed: the thanks dropped

sentences.display: Ō Mārce, avē. Grātiās tibi agō; bene tibi. Pāx tibi sit atque valē.
sentences.cue: Marcus, hail. I give you my thanks; good health to you. Peace be with you, and farewell.
sentences.literal: O Marcus! hail thanks to-you I-give well to-you peace to-you may-it-be and farewell

words.note: 'O' — the particle of address.
'Marcus' as address — M2's vocative in its formal use.
'Hail' — a greeting for an arrival, and the formal counterpart of L1-M2's salvē. With valē it is Catullus's farewell to his brother.
'Thanks' — plural always. L1-M2's word.
'To you' — the dative, and it appears three times in this sentence.
'I do' — and with grātiās, 'I give thanks'.
'Well'. L1-M2's adverb, and here a toast.
'Peace' as the subject.
'May it be' — sum's present subjunctive, used as a wish.
'And' — L1-M10's heavier conjunction.
'Be well' — L1-M2's word, closing the occasion as it opened this course's second module.

sentences.trap: A whole occasion, and the dative three times. Greeting, thanks, toast, blessing, farewell — five formal moves, and the only words in it this module taught are avē, pāx and requiēscat's mood. Everything else has been available since L1-M2, which is the point: a register is an arrangement, not a vocabulary.
sentences.sound: Nineteen syllables in five moves. Read it as five, and every one of them ends on a long vowel.
